theme: Gulf Type and other round seals: catalogue joins, image-checked transcriptions, shared sequence tradition and twins-initial count
question: Can the Lipi records of round seals be joined to Laursen's 2010 Gulf Type catalogue and to CISI, do their transcriptions agree with published images, do round-seal texts form a shared sequence tradition, and does the twins-initial pattern of West Asian texts hold with image-checked identifications?
outcome: 31 Lipi records joined with evidence (15 by identifier or citation), including 25 of Laursen's 27 Indus-inscribed Gulf Type seals; CISI numbers exist only for the Indus Valley seals (C-32, M-415, M-416, M-417, M-1369, M-1370). Of 137 checked circular-seal sign positions, 2 differ from Lipi; two Gulf seals are coded in mirror order and Lipi codes pseudo-script strokes as numerals. Other round seals predict a held-out round seal 1.28 bits per transition better than matched South Asian text (interval 0.82-1.76, p = 0.001), of which 1.22 bits come from sign frequencies; shared transitions +2.8 points (p = 0.27) against +24.8 for the copper-tablet control. West Asian and South Asian circular seals do not predict each other after Holm correction. Twins-initial: 4 of 22 West Asian texts against 2 of 2,122 South Asian texts, both readers agreeing on all 28 items (Fisher p = 1.2e-7); 2 of 19 without pseudo-inscriptions (p = 0.00044).
challenge: Small regional samples; witnesses are mostly published drawings and 1932 halftones; Reader 1 was not blind to codes; British Museum images unavailable; Lipi's direction field and sign order conflict with the impressions for three Gulf seals; the inventory result admits several explanations (another language, imitation, transcription convention).
remedy: Frozen protocol with hashes, dated amendment before computation, blinded second reader, structure-matched South Asian models and nulls, positive controls, five sensitivities including re-oriented and checked transcriptions, and an independent verifier (14 of 14 checks).
retry_when: Photographs of the Bahrain, Failaka and British Museum Ur seals, Gulf seals found since 2010, or a simulation that separates imitation from names written with chosen signs become available.
